Banks and other infrastructure should be on closed intranets, with access only to account holders and employees, which would seamlessly maintain the convenience of online banking and remote control of power and communication grids for those who desire or need it. Water plants, electric power generators and grids, banks, and supermarket freezers have been around long before the Internet was born, and they were doing just fine (if not better) without it.

By avocation and education a historian, I have long viewed our species with a deep sense of gloom. We seem adept at finding newer, more effective ways of killing each other, other species, the planet, even as we also make "progress", in medicine, science, agriculture. 

Maybe one basic problem is that there are just too many of us, in a world of relatively finite resources. A world we have not made much effort to preserve; rather, we seek ever more ingenious, and frequently dangerous and poisonous, ways to exploit it. 

After having spent the vast majority of my 78 years as an atheist, I was called to the Greek Orthodox faith a few years ago. Now, more than ever, my only hope is God. But for my faith, I would have to believe in humanity. That would be a faith doomed to disappointment, as this marvelous column by Mr. Saslow makes abundantly clear. 

My only regret, having as low a regard for our species as I do, is that our adorable and precocious 8-year old grandson, whom we have done all we can with his Mom to give him an idyllic childhood so far, faces a dystopian future, or none at all. It might have been better had he never been born, so much do I fear what he may face far sooner than later. I feel equally badly for other people finding value in this life. I had a very good one by ordinary standards before becoming disabled 25 years ago. I won't miss it. Most others probably will. But perhaps AI is the Pandora's box we were fated to open...

Ethicists should have been involved from the beginning of AI development. Would the threat of existential doom exist if models had been trained on things other than maximizing profit, efficiency, computational power, etc? Seems to me the problems described here are the problems with capitalism writ large: maximize benefits for the in-group at the expense of everything else. That’s the scenario laid out here in the doomsday fiction - ultimate efficiency will end humanity. But most of us humans actually don’t care all that much about efficiency. We have other reasons to live. 

The models were trained to do this; it did not have to be this way. But since it is, perhaps having some non-mathematicians in the room would be helpful. Perhaps all these nearly identical, highly mathematical men are missing something. Perhaps add in a few philosophers, writers, human rights leaders - people who wrestle with humanity’s darkest impulses and seek the light, non-mathematically. We always listened to the evening news and when the story came we were at the kitchen table eating dinner; my mother pushed her plate away, quickly went into the downstairs bathroom, and threw up. He was a filthy rich Wall Street broker; offensive, intrusive, arrogant, demanding. She was a stay at home wife and mother of their 5 children; emotionally abused and angry. They were both determined to settle the score (whatever they was), with shouting matches each afternoon at the tennis courts. Both served as well as they received. A Saturday and Sunday spectacle in south Florida until they flew back to NY in a private jet. Kids in tow and witness to this soap opera each and every day.  "War" understates real life, just the way "House of Cards" seemed over-the-top until Trump took over the White House. Reality is a bitter pill to shallow not matter how sweet the entertainment industry tries to make it. Bicycle helmet Lost & Found: I was born in the 1950s & spent the first half of my life in Greenwich Village/Chelsea.
Biked EVERYWHERE. Didn't even see a bike helmet until the early 80s. We rode everywhere on our steel bikes, dodging buses and cabs un-helmeted. 
Some road racers wore head gear made of padded leather strips -but the joke was the most that might do was keep the brains in one place after a bad crash.
Another popular item were the small caps with a narrow visor (still popular with "roadies") that contained sweat & almost shielded the eyes from sun. Ironically they were called "casquettes"
I spotted my first Mountain Bike in the mid 1980s -and that was a revelation which altered my life's trajectory. We began wearing the contoured foam helmets that were available at the time.
My mtb mentor spoke of the early "mountain bike pioneers" in northern California. It didn't take long to pack up, & head west (1989), ultimately settling in the tiny town of Fairfax CA -"Birthplace of Mountain Biking". 
I eventually became the volunteer event producer at Marin Museum of Bicycling/Mountain Bike Hall of Fame, winning the friendship & respect of the actual Pioneers of Mountain Biking.
I couldn't count how many helmets I've had in the last 40yrs. & remain concession free!

"Josh Bivens, the chief economist at the Economic Policy Institute, a pro-labor think tank, said unattended factories were “not the thing that keeps me up at night,” because it’s difficult to stop automation once companies begin making upgrades.
He said the United States should increase its social safety net to better cover workers displaced by such technological advances. “We don’t have to have the concentrated costs of it borne so heavily” on workers, he said."

And that's really the nub of one problem automation causes - especially as we're constantly being promised that computational gains and improved robotics will do more and more of the actual work of producing things.

Safety nets based on taxes taken from the human workforce and the companies hiring humans will keep sliding into inadequacy as we create an older, possibly lower-employment future.  Yet the companies that reduce labor, or that don't hire at all, are making money selling stuff they produce.

When are we going to fund safety nets more equably by switching away from the basis of "how many humans * their wage rates" into "our economy is this productive, so fund safety net from productivity".

The other problem is what happens with displaced workers who gain a lot of the structure of their life, and their feeling of contributing, when there's not that type of work anymore and paying to learn new work is a crapshoot at best today, often coming from the pocket of the unemployed worker.

Bankers and investors matter, but when they start sucking up too great a share of the brightest minds, there are fewer and fewer opportunities (especially domestic ones) worth investing in, and more and more money chases value extraction for the benefit of the investor class vs value creation that benefits of society.

As personal wealth and “status” displace the achievement of societal “goods” as goals, we become a society of people who are pursuing personal sugar highs that too often leave us feeling personally and collectively empty.  

When people focus on the sugar highs, even doing the hard work required to get into and graduate from top schools can become more about pursuing labels than learning — about polishing surfaces over building substance.
